# Julia essentials for modelers {#sec-julia-essentials}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 1, Session 1. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd).
:::

This prerequisite equips you with the specific slice of Julia that the rest of
the course depends on: functions with in-place mutation, broadcasting and
comprehensions, named tuples for model parameters, multiple dispatch, and
reproducible random numbers. Rather than surveying the language, we introduce each feature
through the object we return to in every chapter — the susceptible–infectious–
recovered (SIR) model of @kermack1927.

Scientific computing has long been split across two languages: a convenient one
for writing the analysis and a fast one for the parts that turn out to be too
slow. Julia is designed to be both. It is dynamically typed and interactive like
R, but compiles to native code, so the model kernels you write in this course
are the same code that runs inside the solvers — nothing is rewritten in C to
make it fast enough. That matters here because epidemic models are run
thousands of times over, in stochastic ensembles, sensitivity sweeps, and
inference.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Coming from R?

Most of what you know transfers directly. Assignment uses `=` rather than `<-`,
and indexing starts at 1 as it does in R.

| R | Julia | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `f <- function(x) x^2` | `f(x) = x^2` | or `function f(x) ... end` |
| `x <- c(1, 2, 3)` | `x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]` | `1.0` and `1` are different types |
| `v[1]` | `v[1]` | indexing starts at 1, as in R |
| `m[2, ]` | `m[2, :]` | row 2, every column; `:` is all of a dimension |
| `sapply(v, f)` | `f.(v)` | the dot applies `f` elementwise |
| `sapply(1:5, f)` | `[f(k) for k in 1:5]` | a comprehension builds a vector |
| `x[x < 0.5]` | `x[x .< 0.5]` | comparisons need the dot too |
| `for (i in 1:10)` | `for i in 1:10 ... end` | no brackets, closed with `end` |
| `list(a = 1, b = 2)` | `(a = 1, b = 2)` | a named tuple; read fields with `p.a` |
| `rbinom(1, n, prob)` | `rand(Binomial(n, prob))` | build the distribution, then draw |
| `TRUE` / `FALSE` | `true` / `false` | lowercase |

An R named list also translates to a `Dict`, `Dict("a" => 1)`, read with
`d["a"]`; this course uses named tuples for model parameters because their field
names are known to the compiler. The official
[noteworthy differences from R](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/noteworthy-differences/#Noteworthy-differences-from-R)
is the complete list.
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this unit you should be able to:

- read and write Julia functions that mutate a preallocated array in place, the
  pattern every SciML solver expects;
- use broadcasting (`.`) and comprehensions to vectorise scalar operations
  without writing loops;
- group model parameters in a `NamedTuple` and access them by field rather than
  by position;
- collect results with a loop and `push!` or into a preallocated array, and
  build a variant parameter set with `merge`;
- recognise that Julia resolves a function by the *types* of its arguments, and
  explain why that is what lets `solve` accept any problem/algorithm pair;
- produce bit-for-bit reproducible stochastic output with `StableRNGs`;
- render a figure from code with `CairoMakie`.

## Model assumptions and classification

The running example is the deterministic SIR model. It assumes a closed,
well-mixed population of fixed size $N$, split into susceptible $S$, infectious
$I$, and recovered $R$ compartments. Individuals mix homogeneously, each
contacting others at rate $c$; a contact between a susceptible and an infectious
individual transmits with probability $\beta$; infectious individuals recover at
constant rate $\gamma$ and are then permanently immune.

| Property | Classification |
|---|---|
| Determinism | Deterministic |
| Time | Continuous |
| State | Continuous |
| Representation | Population (compartmental) |

We do not solve the model here — that is @sec-foundations. In this unit the
model is a vehicle for the Julia constructs you will reuse throughout.

## Equations

The force of infection is $\lambda(t) = \beta c I(t)/N$, and the compartmental
rates of change are

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\lambda S, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \lambda S - \gamma I, \qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} = \gamma I.
$$ {#eq-p01-sir}

Because the three right-hand sides sum to zero, the total population is a
conserved quantity:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(S + I + R\right) = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S(t) + I(t) + R(t) = N.
$$ {#eq-p01-conservation}

When we later discretise time we will need to turn a continuous rate $r$ into
the probability that at least one event occurs in a window of length $\delta t$,
assuming events follow a Poisson process:

$$
p(r, \delta t) = 1 - e^{-r\,\delta t}.
$$ {#eq-p01-rate}

## Julia implementation

We use the course baseline scenario $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, $N=1000$,
$c=10$, $\beta=0.05$, $\gamma=0.25$.

### The REPL and its modes

Julia's read–eval–print loop is the interactive prompt you get by running
`julia`, and it plays the role the console plays in R. What is unusual is that
it has four modes rather than one. Each is entered by typing a single character
at an empty `julia>` prompt, and left again with `Backspace`:

| Key | Mode | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| — | Julia | evaluating expressions; the default |
| `?` | help | `?expm1` prints a function's docstring, signatures, and examples |
| `]` | package | `]st` shows the active environment, `]instantiate` installs it |
| `;` | shell | run `ls`, `cd`, or `git status` without leaving Julia |

```
julia> 2 + 2
4

help?> expm1
  expm1(x)

  Accurately compute exp(x) - 1.

(EpiModelingCourse) pkg> st StableRNGs
Status `~/modeling-epidemics-julia/Project.toml`
  [860ef19b] StableRNGs v1.0.3

shell> ls prerequisites
01-julia-essentials.qmd
```

The prompt in package mode names the *active environment*, and that name is the
first thing to check when a package appears to be missing: the course's packages
are declared in the repository's `Project.toml`, so Julia must be started from
the repository root, or with `julia --project=.`, for `using CairoMakie` to
resolve.

The first `using CairoMakie` in a fresh session takes a minute or more while
Julia compiles the plotting stack, and once per session after that it is fast.
[Setting up](../setup.qmd) covers this and the rest of the installation.

Help mode is worth building a habit around. Every function used in this course
carries a docstring, so `?` answers most "what arguments does this take"
questions faster than a web search, and it works offline on the exact version
you have installed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Typing Greek letters

The course writes parameters as `β`, `γ`, and `λ` so the code matches the
equations. These are ordinary variable names, entered at any Julia prompt or in
an editor with a backslash-name and Tab: `\beta`⇥ gives `β`, `\gamma`⇥ gives
`γ`, `\lambda`⇥ gives `λ`, and `\delta`⇥ gives `δ`. Subscripts work the same
way, and the next chapter uses them for $R_0$ and $s_0$: `R\_0`⇥ gives `R₀` and
`s\_0`⇥ gives `s₀`. ASCII names such as `beta` and `R0` work identically — the
choice is cosmetic.
:::

### Functions and in-place mutation

Every SciML right-hand side has the signature `f(du, u, p, t)`: it *writes* the
derivatives into a preallocated vector `du` and returns nothing. This avoids
allocating a fresh array on each of the thousands of evaluations a solver makes.
Here `u = [S, I, R]` maps directly onto the states in @eq-p01-sir, and `p`
carries $(\beta, c, \gamma, N)$.

```{julia}
#| label: p01-kernel
function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N     # force of infection, λ = βcI/N
    du[1] = -λ * S              # dS/dt
    du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I     # dI/dt
    du[3] = p.γ * I             # dR/dt
    return nothing
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]        # S, I, R
p  = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0)
du = zeros(3)
sir_ode!(du, u0, p, 0.0)
du
```

The trailing `!` is a Julia convention marking a function that mutates its
arguments.

Note the two containers are read in different ways, and this is the convention
the whole course follows. The state `u` is a plain vector whose order is fixed
by @eq-p01-sir, so we destructure it positionally: `S, I, R = u`. The parameters
`p` are a `NamedTuple`, read by field: `p.β`, never `p[1]`. Parameter lists grow
and get reordered as models gain features, and a positional read fails silently
when that happens — the code still runs and every number is wrong. A field name
either resolves or errors.

### Broadcasting and comprehensions

The dot syntax applies a scalar function elementwise, fusing all operations into
a single loop with no temporaries. We use it constantly to evaluate a model over
a grid. Below we compute @eq-p01-rate for a range of window widths and two
rates.

```{julia}
#| label: p01-broadcast
rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)   # numerically stable 1 - exp(-r δt)

δts = 0.0:0.05:2.0
p_fast = rate_to_proportion.(1.0, δts)   # broadcast over δts
p_slow = rate_to_proportion.(0.25, δts)
(first(p_fast), last(p_fast), first(p_slow), last(p_slow))
```

`expm1(x)` computes $e^x - 1$ accurately for small `x`, avoiding the
cancellation error of `1 - exp(...)`.

A *comprehension* is the other way to build a vector from an expression. Where
broadcasting applies one function elementwise, a comprehension can evaluate an
arbitrary expression per element, so it is what we reach for when the body is
more than a single call:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-comprehension
prevalences = [10.0, 100.0, 500.0]
[p.β * p.c * I / p.N for I in prevalences]     # λ at three prevalences
```

Read it right to left: *for each* `I` *in* `prevalences`, evaluate the
expression, and collect the results into a vector. We use comprehensions
throughout the course to sweep a parameter or to pull one compartment out of a
solved model.

### Building and updating containers

Broadcasting and comprehensions cover the case where one expression is applied
to every element. When the body is longer, or when a result has to be assembled
along the way, we write the loop out and collect as we go. An empty typed array
grows with `push!`:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-loop
contact_rates = [4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0]
reproduction_numbers = Float64[]

for c_val in contact_rates
    push!(reproduction_numbers, p.β * c_val / p.γ)   # R₀ = βc/γ
end

reproduction_numbers
```

`Float64[]` is an empty vector whose element type is fixed when it is created.
Plain `[]` gives a `Vector{Any}`, which the compiler cannot specialise on, so the
element type is always worth naming. The loop variable is `c_val` rather than
`c`, because `p.c` is already the contact rate and shadowing it makes the body
harder to read.

When the number of results is known in advance, allocate the array once and fill
it by index. Later chapters store whole trajectories this way, one row per
compartment and one column per scenario or time step:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-preallocate
prevalences = [10.0, 100.0, 500.0]
derivatives = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, length(prevalences))

for (k, I) in enumerate(prevalences)
    sir_ode!(du, [p.N - I, I, 0.0], p, 0.0)
    derivatives[:, k] .= du
end

derivatives
```

`undef` leaves the memory uninitialised, so every entry has to be written before
it is read. `enumerate` pairs each element with its position, which is where the
index `k` comes from. The `.=` copies into the existing column instead of
replacing it, the same in-place idea as `du[1] = ...` above. Reading back,
`derivatives[:, k]` is column `k`, and `derivatives[2, :]` is
$\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t$ at all three prevalences: this row slicing is how the
course pulls one compartment out of a stored trajectory.

A `NamedTuple` cannot be modified in place, so a scenario that changes one
parameter is built with `merge`, which returns a new tuple with the named fields
replaced and the rest carried over:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-merge
p_low = merge(p, (c = 4.0,))
(baseline_c = p.c, low_c = p_low.c, β_carried_over = p_low.β == p.β)
```

The trailing comma in `(c = 4.0,)` is what makes it a one-field named tuple;
without it the brackets are ordinary grouping and `merge` has nothing to merge.
This is how the course varies one parameter at a time, including from inside a
solver callback (@sec-ordinary-differential-equations).

`map` applies a function to each element and collects the results, like a
comprehension with a function in place of the expression. A `do` block writes
the function body after the collection, which keeps a multi-line body readable:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-map-do
sweep = map(contact_rates) do c_val
    p_c = merge(p, (c = c_val,))
    (c = c_val, R₀ = p_c.β * p_c.c / p_c.γ)
end
```

Each iteration returns a small `NamedTuple`, so `sweep` is a vector of rows,
which is the shape a parameter sweep is usually reported in.

The validation cells in every unit ask a question of a whole collection at once.
`all`, `any` and `count` take the test first and the collection second:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-predicates
(any(>(1), reproduction_numbers),
 count(>(1), reproduction_numbers),
 all(v -> isapprox(sum(v), 0.0; atol = 1e-12), eachcol(derivatives)))
```

`>(1)` builds the function "is greater than 1", and `v -> isapprox(...)` is an
anonymous function, written inline because it is needed once. `eachcol` walks
the columns of the matrix, so the third check reads as "the derivatives conserve
population at every prevalence".

### Multiple dispatch

Multiple dispatch lets one function name resolve to different *methods*
depending on the types of its arguments. A method is one concrete
implementation; the function is the name they share. Here `force_of_infection`
accepts either the number infectious or a whole state vector, from which it
reads $I$ itself:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-dispatch
force_of_infection(I::Number, p)         = p.β * p.c * I / p.N
force_of_infection(u::AbstractVector, p) = force_of_infection(u[2], p)

(force_of_infection(10.0, p), force_of_infection(u0, p))
```

`Number` and `AbstractVector` are *abstract* types — categories rather than
concrete containers — so the second method accepts any vector-like argument, not
just the `Vector{Float64}` we happen to pass. Note what dispatch replaces: there
is no `if` inspecting what was passed in, and no extra argument saying which form
the caller used.

You will not often write dispatch in this course, but you will rely on it in
every chapter. When the next chapters call `solve(prob, Tsit5())`, no glue code
connects that problem to that algorithm: `solve` resolves to a method chosen by
the types of *both* arguments. This is why swapping `Tsit5()` for a stiff solver,
or handing the same `ODEProblem` to a sensitivity or inference package, needs no
change to the kernel you wrote. Independently written SciML packages compose
because each adds methods rather than editing anyone else's.

### Reproducible randomness

Later chapters simulate stochastic epidemics. To make figures reproducible we
seed a *local* random stream with `StableRNGs`, whose output is fixed across
Julia versions — unlike the global `Random.default_rng()`.

```{julia}
#| label: p01-rng
using StableRNGs
rng = StableRNG(2024)
draws = rand(rng, 5)
```

### A figure from code

We now visualise @eq-p01-rate with `CairoMakie`. The last expression in the cell
(the `Figure`) is what Quarto renders.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-p01-rate
#| fig-cap: "Probability of at least one event in a window of width $\\delta t$ for a Poisson process, for a fast ($r=1$) and slow ($r=0.25$) rate. Both curves rise from 0 and saturate at 1."
using CairoMakie

fig = Figure(size = (640, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1];
    xlabel = "time step δt",
    ylabel = "event probability  1 − exp(−r δt)",
    title  = "Rate-to-proportion conversion")
lines!(ax, δts, p_fast; linewidth = 3, label = "r = 1.0")
lines!(ax, δts, p_slow; linewidth = 3, label = "r = 0.25")
axislegend(ax; position = :rb)
fig
```

## Validation

Two structural checks confirm the constructs behave as the mathematics
requires.

First, the derivatives in @eq-p01-sir must sum to zero, reproducing the
conservation law @eq-p01-conservation:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-check-conservation
sir_ode!(du, u0, p, 0.0)
isapprox(sum(du), 0.0; atol = 1e-12)
```

Second, `rate_to_proportion` must reduce to its first-order Taylor expansion
$p \approx r\,\delta t$ as $\delta t \to 0$, and must always return a valid
probability in $[0, 1]$:

```{julia}
#| label: p01-check-rate
small = rate_to_proportion(0.25, 1e-6)
(isapprox(small, 0.25e-6; rtol = 1e-3), all(0 .<= p_fast .<= 1))
```

Both cells return `true`, so the in-place kernel conserves population and the
rate conversion is well behaved.

## Interpretation and limitations

You now have the exact Julia vocabulary the course relies on: the REPL, in-place
kernels, broadcasting and comprehensions, loops that collect into arrays, named
tuples read by field and updated with `merge`, dispatch, and seeded randomness.
This unit is deliberately narrow: it is not a full Julia tutorial. It does not
cover package management beyond activating and
instantiating the course environment, performance profiling, metaprogramming,
user-defined `struct`s, or the type system's parametric machinery. For those, consult the official
[Julia documentation](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/) and the
[performance tips](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/performance-tips/).
The [CairoMakie documentation](https://docs.makie.org/stable/) covers the
plotting API in depth.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#p01-ex1}

Write an in-place kernel `sir_incidence!(du, u, p, t)` that extends
@eq-p01-sir with a fourth state $C$ tracking *cumulative* infections, so that
$\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}t = \lambda S$. Evaluate the derivative at the baseline
initial condition and confirm that `du[4]` equals `-du[1]` (new infections leave
$S$ at exactly the rate they enter $C$).

### Exercise 2 {#p01-ex2}

Using `StableRNG(2024)`, draw 10 000 samples from `rand`, and use broadcasting
to count how many fall below `rate_to_proportion(0.25, 1.0)`. Compare the
observed fraction with the target probability and explain why a *local* seeded
RNG makes this figure reproducible across machines.
